profile.name: Sandee Srisawat
profile.headline: Building the systems behind the play.
profile.intro: I’m a game programmer interested in creating responsive gameplay, reusable systems that connects, to create memorable player experiences.
profile.about: I’m interested in the details that make a game feel good to play: responsive controls, thoughtful interactions, and systems that work together.
profile.approach: I enjoy building responsive movement and combat systems, refining them through playtesting until they feel satisfying. I approach difficult problems by breaking them into smaller parts and testing one change at a time, while building reusable components that make new features easier to add. Gameplay programming draws me in because it combines technical problem-solving with creating experiences players can feel.

projects.title: Project SeaShelt
projects.description: A mobile game commissioned for an event, developed in Unity. I worked as a freelance game developer, designing levels and implementing gameplay systems including health, armor, obstacles, and sun exposure with protective shade.
projects.overview: This is a sample project breakdown, ready for a real project. The prompts below describe what to add; they do not represent completed work or experience.
contributions: Designed levels for a mobile game commissioned for an event.
Built gameplay systems using a component-based architecture.
Implemented a state-machine-driven GameManager to manage game flow.
Implemented player health, armor, and obstacle mechanics.
Created an environmental damage system in which sun exposure damages the player and shade provides protection.

projects.challengesTakeaways:
One challenge was reliably switching sun damage on and off as the player moved between exposed and shaded areas. I placed colliders to define safe areas, preventing sun damage while the player was inside and resuming it when they left.

Another challenge was connecting health, armor, obstacles, and environmental damage without tightly coupling their components. I used an event-driven system so components could react to gameplay events while keeping their responsibilities separate.

projects.title: Excorcism Of Elizabeth
projects.description: I was responsible for designing and implementing the core interaction, inventory, and time-based event systems for Excorcism of Elizabeth, building a modular and multiplaye-architecture that allowed any actor in the world to become interactable without coupling it to the player character.
projects.overview: This is a sample project breakdown, ready for a real project. The prompts below describe what to add; they do not represent completed work or experience.
contributions: Designed and implemented a modular player interaction system using a BPI_Interactable Blueprint Interface and a BPC_PlayerInteractor Actor Component, enabling any actor in the world to become interactable without modifying the player character.

Built a two-handed inventory system with pick up, drop, item mesh swapping, and hand-specific slot tracking, structured to work correctly in a multiplayer environment using Server RPCs and replicated variables.
Designed a time-based event system using BP_TimeManager and BP_BasedTimedActors, allowing world actors such as doors and magic circles to trigger and respond to timed gameplay events.

projects.challengesTakeaways: The biggest challenge was making the interaction system work in multiplayer. Calls made directly from the client on world actors get silently dropped by Unreal since the client doesn't own them. I solved this by moving the Server RPC onto the player's own component, which then calls the interface on the item from the server. This taught me how Unreal's ownership model works and why multiplayer architecture needs to be considered from the start.

projects.title: Zombid - 19
projects.description: I was responsible for designing and implementing the slot-based inventory system for Zombid-19 and integrating a designer-provided gun template with it, extending the system with ammunition management, reloading, weapon switching, and audio/visual feedback.
projects.overview: This is a sample project breakdown, ready for a real project. The prompts below describe what to add; they do not represent completed work or experience.
contributions: Built inventory slot system for storing, stacking, selecting, and using items.
Connected a designer-provided gun template to our inventory, enabling weapon switching and preserving ammunition counts.
Extended the gun system with inventory-based reloading, reload cancellation, and shotgun spread.
Integrated weapon sounds, muzzle flashes, camera shake, and bullet tracers using existing assets and components.
Added reload progress feedback to the player interface.

projects.challengesTakeaways:
With limited time, I extended the gun template and connected it to our custom inventory. This saved development time but required adapting unfamiliar logic.

Incompatible weapon skeletons made muzzle sockets unreliable. I used individually positioned MuzzlePoint components as a practical workaround.

I learned to connect separate gameplay systems, handle interrupted actions, and prioritise features within our deadline.
